chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 341 to 350, Othalanthaiyar's paalai decade of early spring (இளவேனிற் பத்து): every poem opens on the same line, he does not come but the time has come, and closes on one sign of spring (the koel, drunk bees on the nunavam, the kongu bud, punku leaves on young breasts, the kadamba grove, the paathiri, the mango's flame-red shoots, the neem), until the last names it as the time his sweet words had promised.

341.reading: She says that he has not come, but the time has come, the time when the female koel calls in her sweet voice and the fine sand-ripples, the colour of grit, sway in the thinning stream.
341.nuance: The refrain sets two subjects against each other: அவர் (he) does not come, தான் (it, the time) has come of itself. The poet chose the female koel, the calling mate, but the poem gives her no answering male, so she is left as a sound of the season rather than an act (scene, not iraicchi); the shrunken stream over fine sand is the first sign of the hot months of paalai.

342.reading: She says that he has not come, but the time has come when the black-stemmed nunavam, its big branches loud with drunken bees, gives out its scent.
342.nuance: The bees are drunk with the season (களித்து ஆலும) while she is sober with waiting; the revel is only a mood, with no act of a lover in it, so it stays scene.

343.reading: She says that he has not come, but the time has come when the beautiful fat buds borne by the firm-standing kongu tree burst open.
343.nuance: உடையும் is the bursting of the bud, a ripeness that cannot be held back: the tree's time, like the season, runs on whether or not he keeps his.

344.reading: She says that he has not come, but the time has come when women smear the tender leaves of the punku, its flowers like puffed rice, on their young breasts to make their beauty shine.
344.nuance: The season's custom is an adornment for a lover's eyes: the young leaves are worn so that the breasts may be seen, and the one who should see them is away, so the beauty the season makes is wasted on her.

345.reading: She says that he has not come, but the time has come when our fragrant cool grove, roofed over with the right-whorled kadamba, breaks into flower.
345.nuance: நம் makes the grove theirs: the place that blooms is the one they shared, so the spring is not only a date he has missed but a meeting place that keeps its appointment without him.

346.reading: She says that he has not come, but the time has come when, the paathiri on its lovely branches having blossomed, the dark red-eyed koel cries aloud.
346.nuance: அறையும் is to cry out as a drum proclaims: the koel announces the season the paathiri has opened, so the bird is a herald of the date, and its announcement is public while her waiting is private.

349.reading: She says that he has not come, but the time has come when the mango with its cracked bark puts out young shoots like flame, so many that its branches are buried in them.
349.nuance: பொரிகால் and எரிகால் rhyme across the two lines: the old trunk looks scorched and the new shoots look like fire, so the tree that seemed burnt out renews itself, which is what the parted woman cannot do.

350.reading: She says that he has not come, but the time has come, the time of the neem's bright flowers crowding the branches, the very time of which he assured us with honey-sweet words.
350.nuance: The last poem names what the refrain has meant all along: the time that has come is the time his own sweet words fixed (தெளிக்கும், to make one sure), so the decade ends on a broken assurance, not on a season. The neem is the bitter tree, and its bright flower stands beside the honeyed words.

links.note: Every poem of the decade says the time has come (தான் வந்தன்றே); 350 says it is the time of which he assured them with sweet words (தேம்படு கிளவி ... தெளிக்கும் பொழுதே).
links.teaches: Read from 350 back to 341, the unnamed 'it' of the refrain turns out to be his promised date, so each spring sign in the decade is a clause of his oath being checked off, not a description of the season.

links.note: Akananuru 355 says spring has come of itself (செவ்விவேனில் தானே வந்தன்று) to a woman whose man is about to leave; the Ainkurunuru refrain says the same with தான் வந்தன்றே after he has gone.
links.teaches: The same formula serves first as the woman's argument against going, the season lovers spend in cool groves, and then as the proof that he went anyway, so 'it came of itself' carries the reproach that the season keeps its time unasked while the man does not.

links.note: Akananuru 355 says in spring lovers stay in the cool grove of dropping pollen and forget their rich homes (தண்பொழில் அல்கிக் காதலர் செழுமனை மறக்கும்); Ainkurunuru 345 says our fragrant cool grove (நம் மணங்கமழ் தண்பொழில்) is in bloom.
links.teaches: Akananuru 355 supplies the custom that the four-line poem leaves out: the flowering grove is where lovers spend spring together, so 'our grove blooms' is an empty place set for two, not a pleasant view.

links.note: In Natrinai 224 the red-eyed dark koel (செங் கண் இருங் குயில்) calls as if saying 'you who are joined, stay joined' before the man leaves; in Ainkurunuru 346 the same koel (செங்கண இருங்குயில்) cries after he has gone and not returned.
links.teaches: One bird in one spring is a plea against parting while the man is still at home and an announcement of his failure once he is away, so the koel's call has no fixed sense of its own and takes its meaning from the stage of the parting.

links.note: Natrinai 224 sets 'sweet spring has come' (இன்ப வேனிலும் வந்தன்று) beside 'those who assured us we will not part' (பிரியலம் என்று தெளித்தோர்); Ainkurunuru 350 ends with the time of which he assured them (தெளிக்கும் பொழுதே).
links.teaches: Natrinai uses தெளித்தல் for the man's sworn assurance in the very poem where spring arrives, which supports reading Ainkurunuru 350's தெளிக்கும் as his promise, and shows that spring's coming and the lover's oath were a fixed pair in paalai poetry.

links.note: In Akananuru 317 the man's quoted promise names the spring signs, the koel in the mango and the kongu and kuravam dropping flowers, and he arrives on time; in Ainkurunuru 350 the time of his assurance comes and he does not.
links.teaches: Akananuru 317 shows that the catalogue of spring flowers and birds was itself the wording of the man's promise, so the Ainkurunuru decade's list of the same signs is the promise read back to an absent man, and 317's ending is the one the decade is denied.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 4's friend calls the season of humming bees and a forest in bloom the medicine for the heroine's pallor (பசலை மருந்து); in Ainkurunuru 342 the bees revel on the flowering nunavam and he has not come.
links.teaches: The friend can call the flowering season a cure only because it guarantees his return; Ainkurunuru 342 shows the same flowering turning into the sickness once the season arrives without him, so the convention's comfort is only as good as the man's timekeeping.

links.note: Kural 1269 says one day is like seven for those who pine with their eyes on the day of return (வருநாள்வைத்து ஏங்குபவர்க்கு); Ainkurunuru 350 is spoken on that day, the time he named, and he has not come.
links.teaches: The couplet measures the waiting before the fixed day as the long part, while the poem shows the fixed day arriving empty, so the Kural's pain has a limit that the Ainkurunuru woman has already passed, when waiting no longer has a date to count toward.

source_issues: 341-350: the colophon has no thurai for this decade; speaker (the wife) and addressee (her friend) are inferred from the refrain, so occasion words are null.
344 line 2: இஅள்முலை is a corrupt form; 347 line 2 has இளமுலை in an otherwise identical line, which is the reading taken.

344 and 347 are word for word the same poem (apart from the corrupt letter), and so are 345 and 348; a ten-poem decade on ten spring signs would not repeat two of them, so the source has probably filled two lost or misread poems with copies of their neighbours. Both pairs are marked as printed.

350 line 3 is a repaired line (tamilvu reading); தேம்படு கிளவியவர்த் தெளிக்கும் is taken as 'the time of which he assured (us) with honeyed words', a reading not fully certain, and line 2's உறப்பத் (crowding, pressing thick) is read with it.
